entry:
Science of naming, defining, and classifying groups of biological organisms on the basis of shared characteristics. The term, from Ancient Greek *taxis* ('arrangement') and *-nomia* ('method'), was introduced in 1813 by de Candolle in his *Théorie élémentaire de la botanique*. Modern approaches prioritize common ancestry and evolutionary relationships.

Organisms are grouped into taxa (singular: taxon), and each group is given a [[Taxonomic rank|taxonomic rank]]; groups of a given rank can be aggregated into a more inclusive group of higher rank, creating a taxonomic hierarchy. The principal ranks in modern use are domain, kingdom, phylum (division is sometimes used in botany instead), class, order, family, genus, and species. The Swedish botanist [[Carl Linnaeus]] is regarded as the founder of the current system. His *Systema Naturae* (1735) introduced [[Binomial nomenclature|binomial nomenclature]], naming organisms by genus and species.

The Linnaean system has since been transformed into a classification intended to reflect the evolutionary relationships among living and extinct organisms. Contemporary taxonomy emphasizes cladistics, which groups organisms into monophyletic clades based on shared derived characters and common ancestry; debate continues over nomenclatural stability versus strict monophyly.

Definitions of the field vary: some place taxonomy within systematics, others reverse the relationship, and sources disagree on whether nomenclature belongs to it. Europeans tend to use "systematics" for the study of [[Biodiversity|biodiversity]], and North Americans "taxonomy". Taxonomy underpins conservation, medicine, and ecology.

Aromatic beverage prepared by infusing hot or boiling water with fresh or cured leaves of [[Camellia sinensis]], an evergreen shrub native to East Asia that originated in the borderlands of southwestern China, northeast India, and northern Myanmar. Tea has a stimulant effect in humans, primarily because of its [[Caffeine|caffeine]] content. After plain drinking water, it is the most widely consumed beverage in the world.

Varieties differ by cultivar, processing, and blend. Leaves undergo varying degrees of oxidation to yield green tea, minimally oxidized; black tea, fully oxidized; and oolong, partially oxidized. Tea is traditionally made by steeping loose leaves in hot water, though tea bags, powdered tea such as matcha, and iced or milk-based forms are also common. The two main cultivated types are Chinese small-leaf (var. *sinensis*) and Assam-type (var. *assamica*).

The earliest credible record of tea drinking dates to the 3rd century AD, in a medical text by the Eastern Han physician Hua Tuo. Tea became a recreational and social beverage in the [[Tang dynasty]], and ceremonial drinking spread to Japan, Korea, and Vietnam. It reached Inner Asia and South Asia along the [[Silk Road]]. Portuguese priests and merchants introduced tea to Europe in the 16th century, and it became fashionable in Western Europe in the 17th. The British later cultivated it on a large scale in colonial India and Ceylon.

Words for tea fall into three groups: *cha*, which entered English in the 1590s via the Portuguese from Cantonese; *tea*, which arrived in the 17th century via the Dutch; and *chai*. China produces over 50% of global output, followed by India, Kenya, and Sri Lanka.

Application of conceptual knowledge to achieve practical goals, especially in a reproducible way. The word also denotes the products of such efforts, both tangible, such as tools and machines, and intangible, such as software. Technology plays a critical role in science, engineering, and everyday life.

The term dates to the early 17th century, when it meant "systematic treatment"; it derives from Greek *tekhnē* ('craft, art') and *-logia* ('study, knowledge'). From the 19th century, continental Europeans used *Technik* (German) or *technique* (French) for a "way of doing" and *Technologie* for the academic study of the "methods of arts and crafts"; English translated both as technology. In the 20th century, with scientific progress and the Second Industrial Revolution, it came to mean the systematic use of knowledge to practical ends.

The earliest known technology is the stone tool. Hominids learned to make the first stone tools about 2 mya (million years ago) by hammering flakes off a pebble, and the practice was refined 75 kya (thousand years ago) into pressure flaking. Evidence points to continuous human use of fire at least 1.5 mya; Charles Darwin described its discovery as "possibly the greatest ever made by man". Fire allowed cooking, which improved nutrient value. The cooking hypothesis holds that cooking promoted growth in hominid brain size, though some researchers find the evidence inconclusive. Hearths dated to 790 kya may have intensified socialization and contributed to the emergence of language. Evidence of clothing dates to 90–120 kya and of shelter to 450 kya.

The [[Neolithic Revolution]] accelerated innovation and social complexity. Polished stone axes allowed large-scale forest clearance and farming, and agriculture fed larger populations. Increased labor specialization, trade, war, and the need for collective action such as irrigation are thought to have contributed to the first cities, such as Uruk, and the first civilizations, such as Sumer. Writing became the basis for history, libraries, schools, and scientific research. Furnaces and bellows enabled smelting of metals; native copper was probably used from about 10 kya, alloys such as bronze and brass appeared about 4,000 BC, and iron alloys such as steel date to around 1,800 BC.

The earliest record of a ship under sail is a Nile boat dating to around 7,000 BC. The Sumerians in Mesopotamia diverted the Tigris and Euphrates by canals and levees for irrigation. The wheel was invented independently in Mesopotamia, the Northern Caucasus, and Central Europe; estimates range from 5,500 to 3,000 BC, with most experts favoring closer to 4,000 BC. Drawings of wheeled carts date from about 3,500 BC.

Later inventions, including the [[Printing press|printing press]], telephone, and the [[Internet]], lowered barriers to communication and ushered in the knowledge economy. Technology contributes to economic development and prosperity but can also cause pollution, resource depletion, and technological unemployment resulting from [[Automation|automation]]. Philosophical and political debates continue over its role, its ethics, and ways to mitigate its downsides.

Transmission of information over a distance by electrical or electronic means, typically through cables, radio waves, or other technologies. Channels may be divided for multiplexing, letting one medium carry several concurrent sessions. Long-distance technologies of the 19th, 20th, and 21st centuries generally use electric power and include the electrical telegraph, [[Telephone|telephone]], [[Television|television]], and [[Radio|radio]]. The term was coined in 1904 by the French engineer and novelist Édouard Estaunié, who defined it as "remote transmission of thought through electricity". Slow methods such as postal mail are excluded from the definition.

Earlier methods included smoke signals, beacons, and homing pigeons; in 1849 Paul Julius Reuter ran a pigeon service carrying stock prices between Aachen and Brussels until the telegraph gap closed. In 1792 Claude Chappe built the first fixed visual telegraph line, between Lille and Paris; the last commercial line was abandoned in 1880. On July 25, 1837, William Fothergill Cooke and Charles Wheatstone demonstrated the first commercial electrical telegraph. [[Samuel Morse]] independently developed a version and a code that was an important advance. Many inventors contributed to the telephone, including [[Alexander Graham Bell]]. [[Guglielmo Marconi]], who won the 1909 Nobel Prize in Physics, led a revolution in wireless communication in the first decade of the 20th century.

Since the 1960s, digital technologies have supplemented voice with data, and the limits of metallic media prompted optical fibre. Mobile networks evolved from 1G analog to 5G. The [[Internet]] is independent of any given medium and has widened global access to services. In the United States, the AT&T monopoly was broken up in 1984; debates persist over natural monopoly in network deployment and the need for antitrust oversight.

Telecommunications device that enables two or more users to converse when too far apart to be easily heard directly. A telephone converts sound, typically the human voice, into electronic signals that travel to another telephone, which reproduces the sound. Its essential elements are a [[Microphone|microphone]] (transmitter) and an earphone (receiver), usually built into a handset; transmission is possible in both directions simultaneously. Calls are placed by entering a telephone number on a keypad or dial. The word derives from Ancient Greek *tēle* ('far') and *phōnē* ('voice').

Credit for the electric telephone is frequently disputed: Charles Bourseul, Antonio Meucci, Johann Philipp Reis, Elisha Gray, and [[Alexander Graham Bell]], among others, have all been credited. In 2002 the U.S. House of Representatives passed a resolution acknowledging Meucci's work. Bell received the first U.S. [[Patent|patent]] for the device on March 7, 1876, and made the first successful call to his assistant Thomas Watson three days later. His patent rested on the finding that a fluctuating current reproduced sound best.

The first commercial line, in 1877, linked Boston and Somerville, Massachusetts, and nearly 600,000 telephones were in use across the Bell system by 1900. Direct connections between customers were impractical beyond a few, so manually operated switchboards replaced them; exchanges were eventually joined into an automated worldwide public switched telephone network. On April 3, 1973, Martin Cooper of Motorola made the first handheld [[Mobile phone|mobile phone]] call, and commercial cell phones followed in 1983. Convergence with computing produced the [[Smartphone|smartphone]], now the dominant type of telephone.

Instrument for observing distant objects by detecting their emission, absorption, or reflection of electromagnetic radiation. The term originally meant an [[Optical telescope|optical telescope]], using lenses, curved mirrors, or both, but now covers instruments that detect many regions of the [[Electromagnetic spectrum|electromagnetic spectrum]]. The word was coined in 1611 by Giovanni Demisiani, from Ancient Greek *tēle* ('far') and *skopein* ('to look or see').

The first practical telescopes were refractors with glass lenses, invented in the Netherlands at the beginning of the 17th century. The earliest record is a 1608 patent application by the spectacle maker Hans Lipperhey; the actual inventor is unknown. [[Galileo Galilei]] built his own version in 1609 and observed Jupiter's moons, the phases of Venus, and the Moon's surface. In 1668 [[Isaac Newton]] built the first practical reflecting telescope, which uses mirrors. Refractors are limited to about 1 meter (39 inches), so most large research telescopes built since the turn of the 20th century are reflectors; the largest have objectives over 10 meters, and 30–40 m designs are under development.

The 20th century brought [[Radio telescope|radio telescopes]] in the 1930s (the first purpose-built one operated in 1937) and infrared telescopes in the 1960s. Because the atmosphere is opaque to most of the spectrum, X-ray and far-infrared observation requires orbit. The [[Hubble Space Telescope]] detects visible, ultraviolet, and near-infrared light, and the Kepler Space Telescope discovered thousands of exoplanets. The [[James Webb Space Telescope]], an infrared instrument, launched on an Ariane 5 from Kourou, French Guiana, on December 25, 2021, and orbits the L2 Lagrange point.

Telecommunication medium for transmitting moving images and sound; the term also denotes the receiving set. Television is a mass medium for advertising, entertainment, news, and sports. The word combines Ancient Greek *tēle* ('far') and Latin *visio* ('sight'); Constantin Perskyi used it in 1900 at the International Congress of Electricity in Paris.

In 1884 Paul Nipkow patented in Berlin the Nipkow disk, a spinning disk with a spiral of holes that scanned an image line by line. Karl Ferdinand Braun developed the [[Cathode ray tube|cathode ray tube]] in 1897. In 1926 [[John Logie Baird]] gave the first public demonstration of a working television system in London, using mechanical scanning; the next year Philo Farnsworth transmitted the first fully electronic image in San Francisco. The BBC began regular electronic broadcasts in 1936.

After [[World War II]], black-and-white broadcasting became popular in the United Kingdom and the United States, and in the 1950s television was the primary medium for influencing public opinion. Color broadcasting was introduced in the mid-1960s in the U.S. and most other developed countries. Signals were first sent by terrestrial transmitter, then also by cable, satellite, and, since the 2000s, the Internet, and transmission shifted from analog to digital. High-definition formats (1080p, 1080i, 720p) supplemented standard definition. In 2013, 79% of the world's households owned a television set. Flat-panel LCD, OLED, and plasma displays replaced CRT screens, and flat screens decisively overtook CRT in the early 2010s. Smart televisions with Internet functions became dominant by the late 2010s, and streaming services such as Netflix expanded access.

Physical quantity expressing relative hotness or coldness, reflecting the average [[Kinetic energy|kinetic energy]] of the particles in a system in classical thermodynamics and kinetic theory. Temperature is important across natural science, including physics, chemistry, Earth science, astronomy, medicine, biology, and metallurgy. It affects the phase and density of materials, the rate of chemical reactions, thermal radiation, and the speed of sound, which in a gas is proportional to the square root of the absolute temperature.

Temperature is measured with a [[Thermometer|thermometer]], calibrated in scales that historically relied on various reference points. The [[Celsius]] scale (°C), used in most of the world, sets 0 °C at the freezing point of water and 100 °C at its boiling point at sea-level atmospheric pressure. The [[Fahrenheit]] scale (°F) is in common use in the United States, with water freezing at 32 °F and boiling at 212 °F. The [[Kelvin]] scale (K) is an absolute scale used predominantly for science; an increment of one degree Celsius equals one kelvin, and the scales differ by an exact offset of 273.15. The kelvin is one of the seven base units of the [[International System of Units]], defined since May 2019 through particle kinetic theory and statistical mechanics.

[[Absolute zero]], 0 K, equals −273.15 °C or −459.67 °F. Under the third law of thermodynamics it can be approached but never reached; the lowest temperature attained experimentally is 38 pK, or 38 trillionths of a kelvin. Matter there still has quantum-mechanical zero-point energy. Negative absolute temperatures exist and are hotter than any positive temperature.

Use of violence against non-combatants to achieve political or ideological aims, generally intended to instill fear and to reach beyond the immediate victims. No definition has gained universal agreement, partly because the term is politically and emotionally charged. The law-of-war expert Richard Baxter wrote that "the term is imprecise; it is ambiguous; and above all, it serves no operative legal purpose." In 2006 over 109 different definitions were estimated to exist. Some definitions confine terrorism to non-state actors, while other scholars include state terrorism, which some contend is the deadlier form.

The word originated in the [[French Revolution]], describing the Jacobin Club's [[Reign of Terror]]; [[Maximilien Robespierre]] declared that "Terror is nothing other than justice, prompt, severe, inflexible", and in 1795 [[Edmund Burke]] denounced the Jacobins for loosing "thousands of those hell-hounds called Terrorists" on France. The terms regained currency in the 1970s through the Palestine Liberation Organization, the Irish Republican Army, the Basque group ETA, and the Red Army Faction. Suicide attacks increased from the 1980s, typified by the [[September 11 attacks]] in 2001.

Left-wing and right-wing organizations, nationalist and religious groups, revolutionaries, and ruling governments have all used terrorism. Attacks often target crowded public places such as airports, shopping centers, and nightlife venues, aiming to undermine confidence in security measures and prompt policy changes. The Global Terrorism Database, maintained by the University of Maryland, College Park, recorded more than 61,000 incidents of non-state terrorism, causing at least 140,000 deaths, between 2000 and 2014.

Any of various fibre-based materials, including fibres, yarns, filaments, threads, and fabrics. The word comes from Latin *textilis* ('woven'). Textiles were originally woven, but other methods developed later, notably [[Knitting|knitting]] and non-woven processes such as felting. Fibres, which may be natural, synthetic, or both, are twisted or laid out into yarn, and yarns are made into fabric by [[Weaving|weaving]], knitting, crocheting, knotting, tatting, or braiding. Natural fibres include [[Cotton|cotton]], [[Wool|wool]], and [[Silk|silk]]; [[Polyester|polyester]] is synthetic. Consumer textiles, such as clothing and furnishings, prioritize aesthetics and comfort; technical textiles, such as geotextiles and medical textiles, prioritize function. Cotton or blend garments can last twenty years or more with regular use and care.

Textiles rarely survive across millennia, so prehistoric evidence consists mostly of spinning and weaving tools. The earliest spinning tool was the spindle, to which a whorl was eventually added; the spinning wheel came later, though historians are unsure whether in China or India. The first clothes, probably animal skins, were worn at least 70,000 years ago. Dyed flax fibres found in a cave in the Republic of Georgia, dated to 34,000 BC, suggest that textile-like materials were made in the Paleolithic.

The textile industry grew out of craft and was sustained by craft guilds. During the [[Industrial Revolution]] it became increasingly mechanized; with the spinning jenny, invented in the United Kingdom in 1765, textile production became the first economic activity to be industrialized. For plain weave, twill, and satin weave, ancient and modern methods differ little. Textile manufacture is the oldest industrial art.
